1.20 Public Law 86-605. This Act authorized the participation of the United States with Mexico in the construction, operation, and maintenance of Amistad Dam and also authorized the construction, operation, and maintenance, on a self-liquidating basis, of a hydroelectric power plant. The Act also provided that the operation for conservation and release of United States share of the waters shall be integrated with other United States water conservation activities on the Rio Grande below Fort Quitman, Texas, in such manner as to provide the maximum feasible amount of water for beneficial use in the United States.
1.21 In authorizing United States participation in the Amistad project, this act also specified that releases of the US share of waters from the dam for domestic, municipal, industrial, and irrigation uses shall be made pursuant to order by the appropriate authority or authorities of the State of Texas, and that the amount of water available for use in the United States below Falcon Dam with Amistad Reservoir operating would not be less than the amount available under existing (1960) conditions of river development. These provisions have been complied with and all water supply releases from Amistad Reservoir (and also from Falcon Reservoir) are made at the direction of the Texas Water Rights Commission and its watermaster.
1.22 Public Law 88-237. The June 18, 1954 Act of Congress as amended by Public Law 88-237, approved December 23, 1963, authorizes and directs the Secretary of the Interior to market hydroelectric power and energy generated at the Amistad and Falcon projects which is available to the United States under the 1944 Water Treaty, and under the existing agreements between the United States and Mexico. The Bureau of Reclamation, designated by the Secretary of the Interior as marketing agent, has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding with the US Section, IBWC for marketing the power and energy generated at Falcon Dam which is not required for its operation. A similar Memorandum of Understanding will be needed for marketing the power and energy generated at Amistad Dam.
1.23 IBWC Minutes. By Minute No. 207, dated June 19, 1958 and subsequently approved by the two Governments, the Commission concurred in the recommendation of the site for Amistad Dam, the reservoir capacities required for flood control, conservation and silt storage, and the type of dam which could be most economically built. Minute No. 210, dated January 12, 1961 subsequently approved by the two Governments provided for: a power unit in each country with each plant having an ultimate maximum capacity of 80,000 kW at minimum head; each country being permitted to construct its own unit at the time or times and in such stages as it deems appropriate, with the understanding that the other country is not obligated to undertake the construction of its unit at any specified time; installation of intakes and penstocks at the time of construction of the dam; each country generate in its own unit for its use and benefit up to one-half of the potential energy; and that the Commission may temporarily authorize either of the two countries to generate for its use and benefit such part of the potential energy belonging to the other country as the latter cannot generate in its own unit, with the understanding that such authorization and use does not establish any right to continue such generation and use.
